newsitem.title: USA: Nader study opposes Staples-Office Depot merger.
newsitem.headline: Nader study opposes Staples-Office Depot merger.

text.p: Ralph Nader's Centre for Study on Responsive Law said Monday it found lower prices where Staples and Office Depot compete with each other, and called on the government to prevent their merger.

The Federal Trade Commission is considering whether a proposed merger of the companies is legal under the nation's antitrust laws. Staples and Office Depot announced their proposed merger last fall but the FTC has delayed a final decision and requested further documents, the companies say.

Nader and his colleagues said their econometric study, conducted Feb. 20 and 21 at 15 randomly selected Staples and 17 randomly selected Office Depot stores, showed a variation in the price of fax paper.
They said they believe the merger is a bad deal for consumers.

"Office Depot told us that the price for this item was uniform throughout the country, but in the 17 Office Depot locations surveyed we found six different prices, ranging from $19.99 to $27.99, a difference of 40 percent," the study said.
At Staples, the survey found prices raning from $13.99 to $27.99, "a difference of 97 percent," the survey said.

Nader and his group said their study found "competition between Staples and Office Depot particularly important in lowering prices. These data are evidence that the proposed merger will result in higher prices and harm consumers."
In a letter to the FTC, the Nader group said its study cast a new light on the proposal.

"We believe the Staples/Office Depot Merger ... is illegal under the Clayton Act," wrote Nader, James Love and Robert Wiesman of the Center's Consumer Project on Technology. "As consumers of both Office Depot and Staples, we urge the commission to reject the merger." The Clayton Act is the nation's premier antitrust law.
In their letter, Nader and his colleagues also asked to meet with the FTC to present their data.
A spokesman for Staples had no immediate comment and said the company had not seen the survey.
"I'd have to see the survey and find out if it is statistically relevant," Sam Levenson, director of investment relations for Staples, said from the company's Westboroguh, Mass., headquarters.
A spokeswoman for the Federal Trade Commission also had no comment. David Lawsky, Washington newsroom, 202-898-8463.
